claim: Yeast chromatin assembly factor 1 (CAF1) binds a single H3-H4 heterodimer in solution.
source: Here, we report that yeast chromatin assembly factor 1 (CAF1), a conserved histone chaperone complex that deposits H3-H4 during DNA replication, binds a single H3-H4 heterodimer in solution.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by multiple biophysical measurements (SEC-MALLS, AUC, native MS) presented in the Results section.

claim: A new DNA-binding domain exists in the large Cac1 subunit of CAF1.
source: We identify a new DNA-binding domain in the large Cac1 subunit of CAF1, which is required for high-affinity DNA binding by the CAF1 three-subunit complex, and which is distinct from the previously described C-terminal winged-helix domain.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, supported by DNA-binding assays with deletion mutants shown in Figure 3.

claim: CAF1 binds preferentially to DNA molecules longer than 40 bp.
source: CAF1 binds preferentially to DNA molecules longer than 40 bp, and two CAF1-H3-H4 complexes concertedly associate with DNA molecules of this size, resulting in deposition of H3-H4 tetramers.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by DNA-binding assays with different DNA lengths shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Two CAF1-H3-H4 complexes concertedly associate with DNA molecules longer than 40 bp, resulting in deposition of H3-H4 tetramers.
source: CAF1 binds preferentially to DNA molecules longer than 40 bp, and two CAF1-H3-H4 complexes concertedly associate with DNA molecules of this size, resulting in deposition of H3-H4 tetramers.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by cooperative binding data (Hill coefficient of 2.0) and tetrasome deposition assays.

claim: DNA binding is not essential for H3–H4 tetrasome deposition in vitro.
source: While DNA binding is not essential for H3–H4 tetrasome deposition in vitro, it is required for efficient DNA synthesis-coupled nucleosome assembly.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by tetrasome deposition assays with DNA-binding deficient mutants shown in Figure 4.

claim: DNA binding is required for efficient DNA synthesis-coupled nucleosome assembly.
source: While DNA binding is not essential for H3–H4 tetrasome deposition in vitro, it is required for efficient DNA synthesis-coupled nucleosome assembly.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by Xenopus egg extract assembly assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: Mutant histones with impaired H3-H4 tetramerization interactions fail to release from CAF1.
source: Mutant histones with impaired H3-H4 tetramerization interactions fail to release from CAF1, indicating that DNA deposition of H3-H4 tetramers by CAF1 requires a hierarchical cooperation between DNA binding, H3-H4 deposition and histone tetramerization.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by deposition assays with H3M-H4 mutant shown in Figure 4C.

claim: DNA deposition of H3-H4 tetramers by CAF1 requires a hierarchical cooperation between DNA binding, H3-H4 deposition and histone tetramerization.
source: Mutant histones with impaired H3-H4 tetramerization interactions fail to release from CAF1, indicating that DNA deposition of H3-H4 tetramers by CAF1 requires a hierarchical cooperation between DNA binding, H3-H4 deposition and histone tetramerization.
evidence: The abstract states this as an interpretation of the H3M-H4 mutant data.

claim: Nucleosomes are composed of an octameric core of histones, around which 147 bp of DNA are wrapped.
source: They are composed of an octameric core of histones, around which 147 bp of DNA are wrapped (Luger et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Luger et al., 1997.

claim: The majority of nucleosomes in chromatin contain two copies of each of the four major histones H2A, H2B, H3 and H4.
source: The majority of nucleosomes in chromatin contain two copies of each of the four major histones H2A, H2B, H3 and H4 that are assembled in a step-wise manner (Smith and Stillman, 1991).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Smith and Stillman, 1991.

claim: Nucleosomes are assembled in a step-wise manner, with H3-H4 tetramer deposited first, followed by two H2A-H2B dimers.
source: The majority of nucleosomes in chromatin contain two copies of each of the four major histones H2A, H2B, H3 and H4 that are assembled in a step-wise manner (Smith and Stillman, 1991). Following the initial H3-H4 tetramer, two H2A-H2B dimers are deposited to complete the octameric core particle.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Smith and Stillman, 1991.

claim: Nucleosome assembly is promoted via the action of histone chaperones.
source: Nucleosome assembly is promoted via the action of histone chaperones, (De Koning et al., 2007; Gurard-Levin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to De Koning et al., 2007 and Gurard-Levin et al., 2014.

claim: DNA replication requires doubling of the amount of chromatin through recycling of parental and incorporation of newly synthesized histones.
source: DNA replication requires doubling of the amount of chromatin which is accomplished through recycling of parental and incorporation of newly synthesized histones (Groth, 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Groth, 2009.

claim: Parental H3-H4 are conservatively propagated as tetramers in proliferating cultured cells upon replication.
source: Cumulative evidence supports the model that upon replication, parental H3-H4 are conservatively propagated as tetramers in proliferating cultured cells (Jackson, 1988; Prior et al., 1980).
evidence: This is stated as a model supported by cumulative evidence with citations to Jackson, 1988 and Prior et al., 1980.

claim: Newly deposited H3-H4 tetramers are assembled entirely of new histones.
source: Newly deposited H3-H4 tetramers are assembled entirely of new histones thus precluding the acquisition of new histone modifications based on preexisting parental modifications within the same nucleosome (Katan-Khaykovich and Struhl, 2011; Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Katan-Khaykovich and Struhl, 2011 and Xu et al., 2010.

claim: Asf1 and DAXX bind H3-H4 dimers but not tetramers.
source: A number of histone chaperones including antisilencing function 1 (Asf1) and DAXX bind H3-H4 dimers but not tetramers, indicating that chaperon-mediated tetramer assembly requires a two-step mechanism (Elsässer et al., 2012; English et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2012a; Natsume et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Elsässer et al., 2012; English et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2012a; Natsume et al., 2007.

claim: Asf1 associates with H3-H4 and Mcm2, a subunit of the replicative helicase.
source: Asf1 associates with H3-H4 and Mcm2, a subunit of the replicative helicase (Groth et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Groth et al., 2007.

claim: A crystal structure of the Mcm2-Asf1-H3-H4 complex reveals a 1:1:1:1 stoichiometry.
source: A crystal structure of the complex and binding studies reveal a 1:1:1:1 stoichiometry indicating that dimeric H3-H4 is propagated at replication forks (Huang et al., 2015; Richet et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Huang et al., 2015 and Richet et al., 2015.

claim: CAF1 is a histone chaperone complex that deposits new H3-H4 de novo in a DNA-synthesis-dependent manner.
source: Chromatin assembly factor 1 (CAF1) is a histone chaperone complex that deposits new H3-H4 de novo in a DNA-synthesis-dependent manner (Smith and Stillman, 1989) and is functionally conserved throughout eukaryotes.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Smith and Stillman, 1989.

claim: CAF1 is functionally conserved throughout eukaryotes.
source: Chromatin assembly factor 1 (CAF1) is a histone chaperone complex that deposits new H3-H4 de novo in a DNA-synthesis-dependent manner (Smith and Stillman, 1989) and is functionally conserved throughout eukaryotes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: CAF1 contains three subunits: p150, p60 and p48 (Cac1, Cac2 and Cac3 in Saccharomyces cerevisiae).
source: CAF1 contains three subunits: p150, p60 and p48 (Cac1, Cac2 and Cac3 in Saccharomyces cerevisiae) (Kaufman et al., 1997; Verreault et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Kaufman et al., 1997 and Verreault et al., 1996.

claim: CAF1 is recruited to the replication fork by interaction of the p150 subunit with PCNA.
source: CAF1 is recruited to the replication fork by interaction of the p150 subunit with proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA), the DNA polymerase processivity clamp (Gérard et al., 2006; Shibahara and Stillman, 1999).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Gérard et al., 2006 and Shibahara and Stillman, 1999.

claim: Human CAF1 preferentially interacts with the replication-dependent histones H3.1/2 but not with the replication-independent histone variant H3.3.
source: Human CAF1 preferentially interacts with the replication-dependent histones H3.1/2 but not with the replication-independent histone variant H3.3 (Benson et al., 2006; Tagami et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Benson et al., 2006 and Tagami et al., 2004.

claim: Budding yeast contains only a H3.3 ortholog which is used in both replication-dependent and independent H3 deposition pathways.
source: Budding yeast contains only a H3.3 ortholog which is used in both replication-dependent and independent H3 deposition pathways.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The C-terminal region of p150 contains a conserved Winged-helix DNA-binding domain (WHD).
source: The C-terminal region of p150 contains a conserved Winged-helix DNA-binding domain (WHD) that is thought to contribute to stabilization of CAF1 at the replication fork (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Zhang et al., 2016.

claim: The p60 subunit preferentially associates with Asf1b in vivo.
source: The p60 subunit preferentially associates with Asf1b in vivo (Abascal et al., 2013; Gurard-Levin et al., 2014; Tagami et al., 2004), and Asf1 is thought to deliver H3-H4 dimers to CAF1 for deposition onto DNA (Tyler et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Abascal et al., 2013; Gurard-Levin et al., 2014; Tagami et al., 2004.

claim: Asf1 is thought to deliver H3-H4 dimers to CAF1 for deposition onto DNA.
source: The p60 subunit preferentially associates with Asf1b in vivo (Abascal et al., 2013; Gurard-Levin et al., 2014; Tagami et al., 2004), and Asf1 is thought to deliver H3-H4 dimers to CAF1 for deposition onto DNA (Tyler et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Tyler et al., 1999.

claim: The p48 subunit interacts with a single H3-H4 dimer through the N-terminal tail of H3 and the N-terminal helix of H4.
source: The p48 subunit (Rb-associated protein RbAp48) interacts with a single H3-H4 dimer through the N-terminal tail of H3 and the N-terminal helix of H4 (Nowak et al., 2011; Schmitges et al., 2011; Song et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Nowak et al., 2011; Schmitges et al., 2011; Song et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: In the context of CAF1, the N-terminal H3 and H4 tails are not essential for histone deposition activity.
source: However, in the context of CAF1, the N-terminal H3 and H4 tails are not essential for histone deposition activity, indicating that additional contacts are made between p150 and/or p60 and the H3-H4 core histone fold (Shibahara et al., 2000; Winkler et al., 2012), a model supported by recent hydrogen/deuterium exchange (HX) data and cross-linking MS (Kim et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Shibahara et al., 2000 and Winkler et al., 2012.

claim: Human CAF1 has been found to bind a single H3-H4 dimer.
source: Human CAF1 has been found to bind a single H3-H4 dimer (Benson et al., 2006; Tagami et al., 2004), whereas yeast CAF1 (yCAF1) has been reported to bind H3-H4 tetramers in a non-canonical conformation in vitro and in vivo and prior to deposition onto DNA (Liu et al., 2012b; Winkler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Benson et al., 2006 and Tagami et al., 2004.

claim: Yeast CAF1 has been reported to bind H3-H4 tetramers in a non-canonical conformation in vitro and in vivo and prior to deposition onto DNA.
source: Human CAF1 has been found to bind a single H3-H4 dimer (Benson et al., 2006; Tagami et al., 2004), whereas yeast CAF1 (yCAF1) has been reported to bind H3-H4 tetramers in a non-canonical conformation in vitro and in vivo and prior to deposition onto DNA (Liu et al., 2012b; Winkler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Liu et al., 2012b and Winkler et al., 2012.

claim: It has been proposed that the Cac1 subunit in isolation is sufficient to enable H3-H4 tetramerization.
source: Further, it has been proposed that the Cac1 subunit in isolation is sufficient to enable H3-H4 tetramerization (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Liu et al., 2016.

claim: All yCAF1 truncation variants were able to bind to Cac2 and Cac3 allowing purification of stable and monodisperse heterotrimeric complexes.
source: We found that all the Cac1 truncation variants were able to bind to Cac2 and Cac3 allowing purification of stable and monodisperse heterotrimeric complexes (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: The Cac1 region required for interaction with Cac2 and Cac3 is located in the segment spanning amino acid residues 230–494.
source: These data show that the Cac1 region required for interaction is located in the segment spanning amino acid residues 230–494.
evidence: This is stated based on the truncation analysis data.

claim: All yCAF1 variants retained the ability to bind H3-H4.
source: All the yCAF1 variants described here retained the ability to bind H3-H4, indicating that the deleted regions of Cac1 are not essential for histone interaction.
evidence: This is stated based on the experimental data with truncation variants.

claim: The deleted regions of Cac1 in the truncation variants are not essential for histone interaction.
source: All the yCAF1 variants described here retained the ability to bind H3-H4, indicating that the deleted regions of Cac1 are not essential for histone interaction.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data showing that all variants bind H3-H4.

claim: The Cac2 and Cac3 binding regions on Cac1 are tentatively assigned to amino acid residues 443–489 and 234–442, respectively.
source: We therefore tentatively assign the Cac2 and Cac3 binding regions on Cac1 to amino acid residues 443–489 and 234–442, respectively.
evidence: This is stated based on limited proteolysis and LC-MS analysis data.

claim: The assignment of the Cac2 and Cac3 binding regions on Cac1 is in agreement with earlier data from yeast and human CAF1.
source: The assignment of the Cac2 and Cac3 binding regions on Cac1 is in agreement with earlier data from yeast and human CAF1 and emphasizes the conserved nature of the CAF1 complex (Kaufman et al., 1995; Krawitz et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Kaufman et al., 1995 and Krawitz et al., 2002.

claim: SEC-MALLS showed a mass of 172 kDa for yCAF1, consistent with the expected mass of a heterotrimer.
source: SEC-MALLS showed a mass of 172 kDa for yCAF1, consistent with the expected mass of a heterotrimer (Figure 1B, Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: In the presence of H3-H4, yCAF1 forms a single species with a mass of 199 kDa, in agreement with binding of one yCAF1 trimer bound to one H3-H4 dimer.
source: In the presence of H3-H4 we found single species with a mass of 199 kDa, in agreement with binding of one yCAF1 trimer bound to one H3-H4 dimer.
evidence: This is stated based on SEC-MALLS data.

claim: yCAF1 binds a single copy of H3-H4 even when H3-H4 was added in twofold molar excess.
source: We obtained the same mass even when H3-H4 was added in twofold molar excess.
evidence: This is stated based on SEC-MALLS data.

claim: All four mutant yCAF1 complexes analyzed formed monodisperse heterotrimers that bound a single copy of H3-H4.
source: All four mutant yCAF1 complexes analyzed also formed monodisperse heterotrimers that bound a single copy of H3-H4 (Figure 1C,D and Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1C, 1D and Table 2.

claim: Native MS of yCAF1 showed an ion population at high m/z corresponding to a mass of 174 kDa, in agreement with the mass of intact yCAF1.
source: Native MS of yCAF1 showed an ion population at high m/z corresponding to a mass of 174 kDa, in agreement with the mass of intact yCAF1 (Figure 1E; Table 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1E and Table 3.

claim: In presence of histones, yCAF1 was bound to a single copy of H3-H4 (201 kDa).
source: In presence of histones, yCAF1 was bound to a single copy of H3-H4 (201 kDa) (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Tandem MS experiments confirmed a 1:1:1:1:1 stoichiometry of the yCAF1-H3-H4 complex.
source: The 32+ ion population of yCAF1-H3-H4 was subjected to tandem MS experiments and confirmed a 1:1:1:1:1 stoichiometry of the yCAF1-H3-H4 complex (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Isolated yCAF1 forms a heterotrimer containing a single copy of each subunit.
source: Thus, consistent with previous results, we found that isolated yCAF1 forms a heterotrimer containing a single copy of each subunit (Liu et al., 2012b; Winkler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated based on the biophysical data and is consistent with previous results cited.

claim: The data do not support the model that yCAF1 binds two H3-H4 heterodimers.
source: However, none of our data support the model that yCAF1 binds two H3-H4 heterodimers.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the biophysical data.

claim: When excess H3-H4 was added to yCAF1, the largest species obtained corresponded to yCAF1 bound to a single H3-H4 heterodimer.
source: To further test this, we added excess H3-H4 to yCAF1 and analyzed the sample by native MS. The largest species obtained corresponded to yCAF1 bound to a single H3-H4 heterodimer (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Isolated H3-H4 forms tetramers in solution at equivalent concentrations.
source: Considering that isolated H3-H4 forms tetramers in solution at equivalent concentrations (Winkler et al., 2012) and in our native MS experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, Table 3), our data suggest that yCAF1 prevents H3-H4 tetramerization.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Winkler et al., 2012 and supported by native MS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and Table 3.

claim: yCAF1 prevents H3-H4 tetramerization.
source: Considering that isolated H3-H4 forms tetramers in solution at equivalent concentrations (Winkler et al., 2012) and in our native MS experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, Table 3), our data suggest that yCAF1 prevents H3-H4 tetramerization.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data showing that yCAF1 binds only one H3-H4 dimer even in the presence of excess H3-H4.

claim: yCAF1 forms an elongated heterotrimer with 1:1:1 stoichiometry.
source: In agreement with recent negative stain electron microscopy data (Kim et al., 2016), we found that yCAF1 forms an elongated heterotrimer containing a single copy of each subunit and that H3-H4 binds in a central position.
evidence: This is stated based on SAXS data showing an elongated particle and is consistent with previous EM data cited.

claim: H3-H4 binds in a central position on yCAF1.
source: In agreement with recent negative stain electron microscopy data (Kim et al., 2016), we found that yCAF1 forms an elongated heterotrimer containing a single copy of each subunit and that H3-H4 binds in a central position.
evidence: This is stated based on SAXS data showing additional mass towards the center of the particle upon H3-H4 binding.

claim: The deletion mapping is in agreement with recent cross-linking MS experiments that indicate that the Cac1 subunit scaffolds interactions with Cac2, Cac3 and histones H3-H4.
source: Our deletion mapping is also in agreement with recent cross-linking MS experiments that indicate that the Cac1 subunit scaffolds interactions with Cac2, Cac3 and histones H3-H4 (Kim et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Kim et al., 2016 and Liu et al., 2016.

claim: The isolated Cac1 subunit is able to interact with H3-H4.
source: As the isolated Cac1 subunit is able to interact with H3-H4 (Liu et al., 2016), our data are in agreement with the model that Cac1 contributes substantially to H3-H4 binding while Cac2 and Cac3 provide accessory interactions.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Liu et al., 2016.

claim: Cac1 contributes substantially to H3-H4 binding while Cac2 and Cac3 provide accessory interactions.
source: As the isolated Cac1 subunit is able to interact with H3-H4 (Liu et al., 2016), our data are in agreement with the model that Cac1 contributes substantially to H3-H4 binding while Cac2 and Cac3 provide accessory interactions.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation consistent with the data and previous findings.

claim: Previous data show that yCAF1 binds two copies of H3-H4 or a covalently crosslinked H3-H4 tetramer with high (KDapp ~5 nM) binding affinity.
source: Previous data are based on fluorescence titration or FRET experiments which show that yCAF1 binds two copies of H3-H4 or a covalently crosslinked H3-H4 tetramer with high (KDapp ~5 nM) binding affinity (Liu et al., 2012b, 2016; Winkler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Liu et al., 2012b, 2016 and Winkler et al., 2012.

claim: High-affinity histone binding by yCAF1 is driven, at least in part, by the highly polar DNA-binding surface of H3-H4.
source: Our data suggest that high-affinity histone binding by yCAF1 is driven, at least in part, by the highly polar DNA-binding surface of H3-H4.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data.

claim: yCAF1 can receive H3-H4 from Asf1 or Mcm2 without forming a stable higher-order complex among these histone chaperones.
source: We found that yCAF1 can receive H3-H4 from Asf1 or Mcm2 without forming a stable higher-order complex among these histone chaperones (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by SEC-MALLS data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The WHD domain is not sufficient for high-affinity DNA binding by yCAF1.
source: In agreement, point mutations that abolish DNA binding of the isolated WHD do not abolish DNA binding by yCAF1 (Zhang et al., 2016). Nevertheless, the WHD clearly contributes to overall yCAF1 activity and might play a role in transcriptional silencing activity and the DNA damage response presumably by aiding recruitment of yCAF1 to replication forks (Liu et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Zhang et al., 2016 and Liu et al., 2016.

claim: High affinity DNA binding by yCAF1 requires a second DNA-binding element located to amino acid residues 135–230 of Cac1.
source: High affinity DNA binding by yCAF1 requires a second DNA-binding element that we locate to the amino acid residues 135–230 of Cac1, a region containing the K/E/R domain and is predicted to form a coiled-coil.
evidence: This is stated based on DNA-binding assays with deletion mutants.

claim: A deletion mutant of human p150 spanning amino acids 311–445 abolishes chromatin assembly activity.
source: This region is also critical in human p150, as a deletion mutant spanning the equivalent region (amino acids 311–445) abolishes chromatin assembly activity (Kaufman et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Kaufman et al., 1995.

claim: yCAF1T and yCAF1V are deficient in DNA interaction but retain H3-H4-binding activity.
source: We identified two mutants, yCAF1T and yCAF1V, that were deficient in DNA interaction but that retained H3-H4-binding activity.
evidence: This is stated based on DNA-binding and histone-binding assays.

claim: The WHD appears to be inert for DNA binding in yCAF1T.
source: Counterintuitively, the WHD appears to be inert for DNA binding in yCAF1T (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated based on DNA-binding assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: H3-H4 binding to yCAF1 could result in unmasking of the DNA-binding activity of the WHD.
source: Previous hydrogen/deuterium exchange (HX) data indicate that H3-H4 binding results in structural rearrangements in Cac1 as evidenced by increased HX for amino acids 550–591 (Liu et al., 2016). Thus, H3-H4 binding to yCAF1 could result in unmasking of the DNA-binding activity of the WHD.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on previous HX data cited.

claim: DNA synthesis-dependent chromatin assembly requires the presence of both the coiled-coil K/E/R and WHD DNA-binding domains.
source: However DNA synthesis-dependent chromatin assembly requires the presence of both the coiled-coil K/E/R and WHD DNA-binding domains.
evidence: This is stated based on Xenopus egg extract assembly assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: yCAF1 binds preferentially to DNA of 40–80 bp length.
source: yCAF1 binds preferentially to DNA of 40–80 bp length and we find that binding to such extended DNA elements is cooperative.
evidence: This is stated based on DNA-binding assays with different DNA lengths.

claim: Binding of yCAF1 to extended DNA elements (40-80 bp) is cooperative.
source: yCAF1 binds preferentially to DNA of 40–80 bp length and we find that binding to such extended DNA elements is cooperative.
evidence: This is stated based on Hill coefficient analysis of DNA-binding data.

claim: Assembly of H3-H4 tetrasomes requires a DNA substrate of ~60–80 bp length.
source: Assembly of H3-H4 tetrasomes requires a DNA substrate of similar length ~60–80 bp (Luger et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Luger et al., 1997.

claim: There is no evidence for yCAF1 or yCAF1-H3-H4 dimerization in solution.
source: Cooperative binding usually requires some form of interaction between binding partners but we do not find evidence for yCAF1 or yCAF1-H3-H4 dimerization in solution.
evidence: This is stated based on the biophysical data showing monomeric complexes.

claim: The isolated Cac1 subunit and the p150 ortholog have a tendency to dimerize in the absence of their binding partners.
source: Previous studies have indicated, that the isolated Cac1 subunit and the p150 ortholog, have a tendency to dimerize in the absence of their binding partners (Gérard et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2016; Quivy et al., 2001; Winkler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Gérard et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2016; Quivy et al., 2001; Winkler et al., 2012.

claim: A C-terminal fragment of Cac1 (amino acid residues 385–606) is sufficient to bind H3-H4 and to promote deposition of a H3-H4 tetramer onto DNA.
source: A C-terminal fragment of Cac1, spanning amino acid residues 385–606, is sufficient to bind H3-H4 and to promote deposition of a H3-H4 tetramer onto DNA (Liu et al., 2016), but the physiological relevance of dimerization of isolated Cac1/p150 remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Liu et al., 2016.

claim: yCAF1 binds cooperatively with DNA and when loaded with H3-H4 heterodimers, this results in tetrasome deposition.
source: yCAF1 binds cooperatively with DNA and when loaded with H3-H4 heterodimers, this results in tetrasome deposition.
evidence: This is stated based on DNA-binding and tetrasome deposition assays.

claim: Histone tetramerization gives directionality to the deposition reaction as it is required for histone release from yCAF1.
source: Our model is that histone tetramerization gives directionality to the deposition reaction as it is required for histone release from yCAF1.
evidence: This is stated as a model based on the H3M-H4 mutant data showing failure to release from yCAF1.

claim: H3-H4 tetramers interact with higher binding affinity (~1 nM) with DNA as compared to yCAF1 (~5 nM).
source: H3-H4 tetramers interact with higher binding affinity (~1 nM) with DNA as compared to yCAF1 (~5 nM) (Andrews et al., 2010; Winkler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Andrews et al., 2010 and Winkler et al., 2012.

claim: The H3M-H4 mutant retains high affinity (~5.5 nM) yCAF1 binding.
source: However the H3M-H4 mutant retains high affinity (~5.5 nM) yCAF1 binding (Winkler et al., 2012), likely explaining the failure to release from yCAF1 in a DNA deposition assay (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Winkler et al., 2012 and supported by data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: yCAF1 has a preference for regular B-DNA.
source: yCAF1 has a preference for regular B-DNA as we failed to detect binding to nucleosome core particles that are known to contain DNA with unusual conformational parameters (Luger et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated based on the failure to bind nucleosomes shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: An extended nucleosome-free DNA region of ~250 bp is present behind and ~300 bp ahead of the replication fork.
source: An extended nucleosome-free DNA region of ~250 bp is present behind and ~300 bp ahead of the replication fork (Gasser et al., 1996; Sogo et al., 1986).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Gasser et al., 1996 and Sogo et al., 1986.

claim: Nucleosome assembly occurs as soon as DNA of sufficient length to wrap around the histone octamer core has passed through the replication machinery.
source: Nucleosome assembly occurs as soon as DNA of sufficient length to wrap around the histone octamer core has passed through the replication machinery (Sogo et al., 1986).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Sogo et al., 1986.

claim: The DNA-binding preferences of yCAF1 allow yCAF1 to 'sense' regions of extended nucleosome-free DNA and promote nucleosome assembly preferentially onto the nucleosome-free region of replicating DNA.
source: Thus it is conceivable that the DNA-binding preferences of yCAF1 described here allow yCAF1 to 'sense' regions of extended nucleosome-free DNA and promote nucleosome assembly preferentially onto the nucleosome-free region of replicating DNA.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the DNA-binding preferences observed.

claim: Assembled chromatin contains nucleosomes separated by small linker DNA (~15–20 bp on average in yeast).
source: In contrast, assembled chromatin, which contains nucleosomes separated by small linker DNA (~15–20 bp on average in yeast), would be expected not to allow the yCAF1 binding thereby preventing its action (Radman-Livaja and Rando, 2010).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Radman-Livaja and Rando, 2010.

claim: Direct DNA binding by HIRA and Rtt106 has been proposed.
source: Not unlike what we propose here for yCAF1, direct DNA binding by HIRA and Rtt106, histone chaperone complexes involved in deposition of different H3 variants, has been proposed (Liu et al., 2010; Ray-Gallet et al., 2011; Schneiderman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Liu et al., 2010; Ray-Gallet et al., 2011; Schneiderman et al., 2012.

claim: PCNA acts as the key recruitment vehicle for CAF1 at replication forks.
source: PCNA has long been reported to act as the key recruitment vehicle for CAF1 at replication forks (Moggs et al., 2000; Shibahara and Stillman, 1999; Zhang et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Moggs et al., 2000; Shibahara and Stillman, 1999; Zhang et al., 2000.

claim: Yeast Cac1 contains one PCNA binding site (PIP) that is conserved from yeast to human p150 and is required for interaction with PCNA.
source: Yeast Cac1 contains one PCNA binding site (PIP) that is conserved from yeast to human p150 and is required for interaction with PCNA (Krawitz et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Krawitz et al., 2002.

claim: yCAF1 recruitment to sites of DNA replication requires cooperation between DNA binding and PCNA interaction.
source: We suggest that yCAF1 recruitment to sites of DNA replication requires cooperation between DNA binding and PCNA interaction.
evidence: This is stated as a model based on the data.

claim: Two yCAF1-H3-H4 complexes cooperatively bind to an extended DNA sequence element to deposit H3-H4 tetrasomes.
source: Our data are consistent with a model where two yCAF1-H3-H4 complexes cooperatively bind to an extended DNA sequence element to deposit H3-H4 tetrasomes (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated as a model based on the data and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: In solution, H3-H4 tetramerization in the yCAF1 complex is not permitted, possibly because residues in the H3-H3' dimerization interface are occluded.
source: In solution, H3-H4 tetramerization in the yCAF1 complex is not permitted, possibly because residues in the H3-H3' dimerization interface are occluded.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data showing that yCAF1 binds only one H3-H4 dimer.

claim: H3-H4 binding to yCAF1 or DNA is mutually exclusive.
source: Furthermore, considering that H3-H4 binding to yCAF1 or DNA is mutually exclusive, we propose that yCAF1 interacts with the DNA-binding surface of H3-H4.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation based on the data.

claim: yCAF1 interacts with the DNA-binding surface of H3-H4.
source: Furthermore, considering that H3-H4 binding to yCAF1 or DNA is mutually exclusive, we propose that yCAF1 interacts with the DNA-binding surface of H3-H4.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on the mutually exclusive binding observation.

claim: All the yCAF1 variants analyzed allowed tetrasome assembly using purified components.
source: All the yCAF1 variants analyzed allowed tetrasome assembly using purified components, but the presence of the DNA-binding domains is required for DNA synthesis-coupled nucleosome assembly (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated based on tetrasome deposition assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: The presence of the DNA-binding domains is required for DNA synthesis-coupled nucleosome assembly.
source: All the yCAF1 variants analyzed allowed tetrasome assembly using purified components, but the presence of the DNA-binding domains is required for DNA synthesis-coupled nucleosome assembly (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated based on Xenopus egg extract assembly assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: H3-H4 tetramerization stabilizes the H3-H4 dimers on DNA and triggers the release from yCAF1.
source: H3-H4 tetramerization stabilizes the H3-H4 dimers on DNA and triggers the release from yCAF1 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated based on the H3M-H4 mutant data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: H3-H4 dimers do not assemble as tetramers prior to deposition onto DNA.
source: This model is in agreement with data showing that H3-H4 dimers do not assemble as tetramers prior to deposition onto DNA (Benson et al., 2006; Tagami et al., 2004) and puts forward the importance of a series of coordinated transitions that require the unique DNA-binding properties of yCAF1.
evidence: This is stated with citations to Benson et al., 2006 and Tagami et al., 2004.

claim: yCAF1 forms a stable, monodisperse heterotrimeric complex with 1:1:1 stoichiometry.
source: Expression and purification of this complex yielded a stable, monodisperse heterotrimeric yCAF1 complex with 1:1:1 stoichiometry, as judged from size-exclusion chromatography coupled to multi-angle laser light scattering (SEC-MALLS; Figure 1B, Table 1).
evidence: This is stated based on SEC-MALLS data shown in Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: yCAF1 bound to histones H3-H4 has a slightly smaller hydrodynamic radius than yCAF1 alone.
source: This complex was able to bind histones H3-H4 to yield a homogeneous complex that, despite the additional mass, had a slightly smaller hydrodynamic radius as indicated by mobility on the size-exclusion column (see also below).
evidence: This is stated based on SEC-MALLS data.

claim: Cac2 and Cac3 were mostly protease cleavage resistant, while Cac1 was readily cleaved into smaller fragments.
source: In agreement with disorder predictions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), we found that while Cac2 and Cac3 were mostly protease cleavage resistant, Cac1 was readily cleaved into smaller fragments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated based on limited proteolysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: yCAF1 bound to 147 bp DNA with a dissociation constant KD of ~2.1 μM.
source: We found that yCAF1 bound to the 147 bp DNA fragment with a dissociation constant KD of ~2.1 μM (Figure 3A, Table 4).
evidence: This is stated based on DNA-binding assays shown in Figure 3A and Table 4.

claim: Quantitative analysis of the yCAF1-DNA binding reaction showed a Hill coefficient of 2.0, indicative of cooperative binding.
source: Quantitative analysis of the binding reaction showed a Hill coefficient of 2.0, indicative of cooperative binding.
evidence: This is stated based on analysis of DNA-binding data.

claim: yCAF1U had a DNA-binding KD of ~4.1 μM.
source: yCAF1U, a construct lacking the WHD domain had a KD of ~4.1 μM, (Figure 3A, Table 4).
evidence: This is stated based on DNA-binding assays shown in Figure 3A and Table 4.

claim: The non-conserved N-terminal region (amino acids 1–129) of Cac1 did not contribute significantly to DNA binding.
source: The non-conserved N-terminal region (amino acids 1–129) did not contribute significantly to DNA binding as a construct lacking this segment (CAF1X) had similar DNA-binding affinity (5.7 μM).
evidence: This is stated based on DNA-binding assays comparing yCAF1U and yCAF1X.

claim: yCAF1T showed no detectable DNA binding, despite containing the WHD domain.
source: yCAF1T, a variant lacking the N-terminal 229 amino acids including the K/E/R-rich coiled-coil, showed no detectable DNA binding, despite the fact that it contained the WHD domain indicating that the DNA-binding activity of the WHD domain is masked.
evidence: This is stated based on DNA-binding assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The DNA-binding activity of the WHD domain is masked in yCAF1T.
source: yCAF1T, a variant lacking the N-terminal 229 amino acids including the K/E/R-rich coiled-coil, showed no detectable DNA binding, despite the fact that it contained the WHD domain indicating that the DNA-binding activity of the WHD domain is masked.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the DNA-binding data for yCAF1T.

claim: yCAF1V showed no detectable DNA binding.
source: yCAF1V, which contained a deletion of the WHD, showed also no detectable DNA binding (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated based on DNA-binding assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The region spanning the K/E/R-rich coiled-coil segment of Cac1 contains a DNA-binding domain which hierarchically cooperates with the C-terminal WHD for high-affinity DNA binding.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that the region spanning the K/E/R-rich coiled-coil segment of Cac1 contains a DNA-binding domain which appears to hierarchically cooperate with the C-terminal WHD for high-affinity DNA binding as constructs lacking this domain are devoid of DNA binding.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the DNA-binding data with deletion mutants.

claim: The WHD contributes to overall DNA-binding avidity but is not sufficient to enable high affinity binding in the absence of the coiled-coil domain.
source: The WHD contributes to overall DNA-binding avidity but is not sufficient to enable high affinity binding in the absence of the coiled-coil domain.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the DNA-binding data.

claim: yCAF1 bound DNA fragments longer than >40 bp more efficiently than shorter ones.
source: Analysis of the DNA sequence length preferences, using a DNA ladder ranging from 20 to 100 bp DNA size (Table 5), showed that yCAF1 bound DNA fragments longer than >40 bp more efficiently than shorter ones (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is stated based on DNA-binding assays shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: 42 bp and 84 bp DNA were bound cooperatively by yCAF1 (Hill coefficient of 2.2 for both substrates).
source: In agreement with our previous results we observed that while 42 bp and 84 bp DNA were clearly bound cooperatively by yCAF1 (Hill coefficient of 2.2 for both substrates), the 17 bp DNA substrate displayed standard Michaelis-Menten kinetics (Hill coefficient of 1.3) indicative of a single binding site (Table 4).
evidence: This is stated based on DNA-binding assays shown in Figure 3C and Table 4.

claim: The 17 bp DNA substrate displayed standard Michaelis-Menten kinetics (Hill coefficient of 1.3) indicative of a single binding site.
source: In agreement with our previous results we observed that while 42 bp and 84 bp DNA were clearly bound cooperatively by yCAF1 (Hill coefficient of 2.2 for both substrates), the 17 bp DNA substrate displayed standard Michaelis-Menten kinetics (Hill coefficient of 1.3) indicative of a single binding site (Table 4).
evidence: This is stated based on DNA-binding assays shown in Figure 3C and Table 4.

claim: yCAF1 efficiently bound to free B-DNA.
source: Of note, while yCAF1 efficiently bound to free B-DNA, the DNA geometry of the nucleosome core particle, a reaction product of yCAF1-mediated assembly, is not compatible with yCAF1 interaction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated based on DNA-binding assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The DNA geometry of the nucleosome core particle is not compatible with yCAF1 interaction.
source: Of note, while yCAF1 efficiently bound to free B-DNA, the DNA geometry of the nucleosome core particle, a reaction product of yCAF1-mediated assembly, is not compatible with yCAF1 interaction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated based on the failure to bind nucleosomes shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Optimal yCAF1 DNA binding requires regular B-DNA geometry and a minimum of ~40 bp length.
source: Together, our results suggest that yCAF1 uses a two-pronged DNA-binding mode involving the WHD and the coiled-coil segment of Cac1. Optimal yCAF1 DNA binding requires regular B-DNA geometry and a minimum of ~40 bp length.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the DNA-binding data.

claim: Titration of the yCAF1-H3-H4 complex onto DNA showed the appearance of tetrasomes but no apparent disome assembly intermediates.
source: Titration of the yCAF1-H3-H4 complex onto DNA showed the appearance of tetrasomes but no apparent disome assembly intermediates (Figure 4A, left panel, lanes 3–10).
evidence: This is stated based on tetrasome deposition assays shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Addition of DNA resulted in release of H3-H4 from yCAF1 as seen by the appearance of tetrasomes and free yCAF1.
source: In all cases, addition of DNA resulted in release of H3-H4 from yCAF1 as seen by the appearance of tetrasomes and free yCAF1.
evidence: This is stated based on tetrasome deposition assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: yCAF1-H3M-H4 complex was deficient in histone deposition on DNA.
source: This complex was deficient in histone deposition on DNA as seen by a lack of disome or tetrasome deposition. Instead, mostly non-specific binding is seen (Figure 4C, left panel, lanes 4–10).
evidence: This is stated based on tetrasome deposition assays shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The deposition defect of yCAF1-H3M-H4 arose due to a failure to release histones from yCAF1.
source: Apparently this defect arose due to a failure to release histones from yCAF1 (Figure 4C, right panel, lanes 3–9).
evidence: This is stated based on tetrasome deposition assays and gel extraction analysis shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: With wild-type H3-H4, the DNA-bound yCAF1 complex showed yCAF1 but no H3-H4, demonstrating that yCAF1 had released H3-H4.
source: With wild-type H3-H4, the DNA-bound complex (* in Figure 4A, lane 7), showed yCAF1 but no H3-H4 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D, lane 2), showing that yCAF1 had released H3-H4.
evidence: This is stated based on gel extraction analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: With the H3M-H4 mutant, the DNA-bound yCAF1 complex contained H3M-H4, demonstrating that the deposition defect arose due to a failure to release H3-H4 from yCAF1.
source: However with the H3M-H4 mutant, the DNA-bound yCAF1 complex (* in Figure 4C, lane 8) contained H3M-H4 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D, lane 3), demonstrating that the deposition defect arose due to a failure to release H3-H4 from yCAF1.
evidence: This is stated based on gel extraction analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The ability of H3-H4 to tetramerize upon DNA deposition contributes to histone release from yCAF1.
source: Taken together, these results provide compelling evidence that the ability of H3-H4 to tetramerize upon DNA deposition contributes to histone release from yCAF1.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the H3M-H4 mutant data.

claim: Xenopus HSEs enabled DNA synthesis-dependent chromatin assembly when using UV-treated DNA.
source: Indeed, Xenopus HSEs enabled us to follow chromatin assembly independently of the requirement for DNA synthesis when using pBSo (Figure 5A, upper panel, lanes 3, 6) and in a DNA synthesis-dependent manner when using UV-treated DNA pBSuv (Figure 5A, lower panel, lane 6).
evidence: This is stated based on chromatin assembly assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: p150-depleted extracts were unable to assemble chromatin in a DNA synthesis-dependent fashion.
source: Such p150-depleted extracts were unable to assemble chromatin in a DNA synthesis-dependent fashion (Figure 5B, lane 4).
evidence: This is stated based on chromatin assembly assays shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Addition of increasing amounts of yCAF1 rescued DNA synthesis-dependent chromatin assembly in p150-depleted extracts.
source: Here, we report that addition of increasing amounts of yCAF1 rescued DNA synthesis-dependent chromatin assembly (Figure 5B, lane 4–7).
evidence: This is stated based on chromatin assembly assays shown in Figure 5B.

claim: yCAF1T showed residual nucleosome assembly activity.
source: The construct lacking the coiled-coil K/E/R domain (yCAF1T) showed residual nucleosome assembly activity as judged by the relative intensity of supercoiled product (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated based on chromatin assembly assays shown in Figure 5C.

claim: yCAF1U and yCAF1X showed more deficient nucleosome assembly activity than yCAF1T.
source: Constructs lacking the WHD (yCAF1U) or both the N-terminal region and WHD (yCAF1X), showed more deficient nucleosome assembly activity (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated based on chromatin assembly assays shown in Figure 5C.

claim: yCAF1V showed the greatest assembly defect among the mutants tested.
source: yCAF1V, a variant containing a deletion of both the coiled-coil and WHD of Cac1 showed the greatest assembly defect, as judged from the amount of supercoiled plasmid product (labeled I in Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated based on chromatin assembly assays shown in Figure 5C.

claim: yCAF1V was able to interact with PCNA, albeit to a lesser extent than yCAF1 wild-type.
source: A FLAG-pulldown experiment showed that yCAF1V was able to interact with PCNA, albeit to a lesser extent than yCAF1 wild-type (Figure 5-supplemental figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated based on FLAG-pulldown data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The two DNA-binding domains were essential for CAF1 activity as the absence of either domain interfered to different degrees with DNA synthesis-dependent chromatin assembly.
source: The two DNA-binding domains were essential for CAF1 activity as the absence of either domain interfered to different degrees with DNA synthesis-dependent chromatin assembly.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the chromatin assembly data with deletion mutants.

claim: yAsf1 and yCAF1 did not interact under the conditions tested, presumably due to the transient nature of this interaction.
source: yAsf1 and yCAF1 did not interact under these conditions, presumably due to the transient nature of this interaction (Malay et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated based on SEC-MALLS data shown in Figure 6 and with a citation to Malay et al., 2008.

claim: In the presence of H3-H4, yCAF1-H3-H4 and Asf1-H3-H4 were observed but no higher-order complex.
source: In the presence of H3-H4, we observed yCAF1-H3-H4 and Asf1-H3-H4 but no higher-order complex (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated based on SEC-MALLS data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Addition of a fivefold molar excess of preassembled Asf1-H3-H4 to yCAF1 resulted in appearance of a yCAF1-H3-H4 complex, due to transfer of H3-H4 from Asf1 to yCAF1.
source: Addition of a fivefold molar excess of preassembled Asf1-H3-H4 to yCAF1 resulted in appearance of a yCAF1-H3-H4 complex, due to transfer of H3-H4 from Asf1 to yCAF1 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated based on SEC-MALLS data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: yCAF1 is able to receive H3-H4 from Asf1, but there is no stable higher-order complex of these histone chaperones.
source: These data show that yCAF1 is able to receive H3-H4 from Asf1, but that there is no stable higher-order complex of these histone chaperones.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the SEC-MALLS data.

claim: An N-terminal fragment of Mcm2 (amino acid residues 1–160) did not interact directly with yCAF1.
source: An N-terminal fragment of Mcm2, spanning amino acid residues 1–160 and sufficient for H3-H4 binding, also did not interact directly with yCAF1 (Figure 6B, Table 3).
evidence: This is stated based on SEC-MALLS data shown in Figure 6B and Table 6.

claim: In a direct competition assay, H3-H4 interacted preferentially with yCAF1 and Mcm2 migrated in its unbound form.
source: In a direct competition assay, H3-H4 interacted preferentially with yCAF1 and Mcm2 migrated in its unbound form (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated based on SEC-MALLS data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Incubation of a fivefold molar excess of Mcm2-H3-H4 with yCAF1 resulted in transfer of H3-H4 to yCAF1.
source: Incubation of a fivefold molar excess of Mcm2-H3-H4 with yCAF1 resulted in transfer of H3-H4 to yCAF1 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated based on SEC-MALLS data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Addition of equimolar ratios of Mcm2, yAsf1 and yCAF1 followed by addition of H3-H4 led to the formation of yCAF1-H3-H4 and yAsf1-H3-H4-Mcm2 complexes.
source: Finally, addition of equimolar ratios of the three chaperones Mcm2 (1-160), yAsf1 and yCAF1 followed by addition of H3-H4 led to the formation of the yCAF1-H3-H4 and yAsf1-H3-H4-Mcm2 complexes.
evidence: This is stated based on SEC-MALLS data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The molecular masses obtained from SEC-MALLS are compatible with the model that a single H3-H4 dimer is bound to the complexes.
source: Of note, the molecular masses obtained are compatible with the model that a single H3-H4 dimer is bound to the complexes (Table 6).
evidence: This is stated based on SEC-MALLS data shown in Table 6.

claim: yCAF1 forms an elongated particle with a maximum diameter (Dmax) of 26 nm.
source: From these data, we obtained an Rg of 6.39 nm for yCAF1 while the distance distribution function p(r) showed skewed shape characteristic of elongated, multi-domain particles, with a maximum diameter (Dmax) of 26 nm (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated based on SAXS data shown in Figure 2E and Table 1.

claim: For yCAF1-H3-H4, an Rg of 6.02 and a Dmax of 25 nm were obtained.
source: For yCAF1-H3-H4, we obtained an Rg of 6.02 and a Dmax of 25 nm (Figure 2E, Table 1).
evidence: This is stated based on SAXS data shown in Figure 2E and Table 1.

claim: The molecular masses determined from SAXS were 175 kDa (yCAF1) and 203 kDa (yCAF1-H3-H4).
source: The molecular masses determined from SAXS were 175 kDa (yCAF1) and 203 kDa (yCAF1-H3-H4), in close agreement with those determined from orthogonal methods (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated based on SAXS data shown in Table 1.

claim: Ab initio reconstructions showed an elongated particle for yCAF1.
source: Ab initio reconstructions showed an elongated particle for yCAF1 (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated based on SAXS data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: In the H3-H4-bound form, a similar elongated shape was obtained with additional mass towards the center of the particle.
source: In the H3-H4-bound form, a similar elongated shape was obtained with additional mass towards the center of the particle (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated based on SAXS data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Ab initio calculation of the Svedberg coefficients of yCAF1 and yCAF1-H3-H4 using the molecular envelopes obtained from the SAXS experiments match the measured Svedberg values from sedimentation velocity AUC experiments.
source: Ab initio calculation of the Svedberg coefficients of yCAF1 and yCAF1-H3-H4 using the molecular envelopes obtained from the SAXS experiments also match the measured Svedberg values from sedimentation velocity AUC experiments (Table 1), also emphasizing the elongated shape of the particle.
evidence: This is stated based on comparison of SAXS and AUC data shown in Table 1.

claim: For yCAF1T, an Rg of 5.66 nm and a Dmax of 20 nm were obtained.
source: For yCAF1T we obtained an Rg of 5.66 nm and a Dmax of 20 nm and for the H3-H4-bound complex an Rg of 5.10 nm and a Dmax of 17.3 nm (Figure 1D,F and Table 1).
evidence: This is stated based on SAXS data shown in Figure 2D, 2F and Table 1.

claim: For yCAF1T-H3-H4, an Rg of 5.10 nm and a Dmax of 17.3 nm were obtained.
source: For yCAF1T we obtained an Rg of 5.66 nm and a Dmax of 20 nm and for the H3-H4-bound complex an Rg of 5.10 nm and a Dmax of 17.3 nm (Figure 1D,F and Table 1).
evidence: This is stated based on SAXS data shown in Figure 2D, 2F and Table 1.

claim: The bulk of the flexible N-terminal region of Cac1 is located at the N-terminal end of the particle.
source: Based on the overall reduction of the particle diameter of yCAF1T, which matches the expected volume of the flexible N-terminal region of Cac1, we suggest that the bulk of this segment is located there.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the SAXS data comparing yCAF1 and yCAF1T.

claim: The histone heterodimer is positioned towards the center of the yCAF1 particle.
source: Comparison of H3-H4-bound and unbound yCAF1 variants indicates that the histone heterodimer is positioned towards the center of the particle (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated based on SAXS data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: A smaller radius of gyration was consistently observed for the H3-H4-bound yCAF1 complexes, indicative of conformational compaction upon histone binding.
source: We consistently observed, as also shown in SEC-MALLS (Figure 1B), a smaller radius of gyration for the H3-H4-bound yCAF1 complexes, indicative of conformational compaction upon histone binding.
evidence: This is stated based on SAXS and SEC-MALLS data.

claim: A series of rigorous and complementary biophysical techniques led to the conclusion that yCAF1 forms an elongated trimer with 1:1:1 stoichiometry, which binds a single H3-H4 heterodimer.
source: Together, a series of rigorous and complementary biophysical techniques led us to conclude that yCAF1 forms an elongated trimer with 1:1:1 stoichiometry, which binds a single H3-H4 heterodimer.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion from all the biophysical data.

claim: Purification of the yCAF1 complex from insect cells revealed the presence of contaminating nucleic acids and insect cell histones H2A, H2B, H3 and H4.
source: Purification of the yCAF1 complex from insect cells revealed the presence of contaminating nucleic acids and insect cell histones H2A, H2B, H3 and H4 suggesting that yCAF1 potentially directly interacts with nucleosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated based on purification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In a direct competition assay, yCAF1 preferentially interacted with naked DNA but not with nucleosome core particles.
source: Titration of the yCAF1 complex showed that in this direct competition assay, yCAF1 preferentially interacted with the naked DNA but not with the nucleosome core particles (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, lanes 2–8).
evidence: This is stated based on native PAGE analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Surfaces of H3-H4 that are required for yCAF1 binding are buried once these histones are assembled into nucleosomes.
source: Thus, surfaces of H3-H4 that are required for yCAF1 binding are buried once these histones are assembled into nucleosomes.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the nucleosome binding data.
